cases.title: Apex — smaller group pricing exercises
cases.prompt:
Create an executive slide analyzing discount leakage across Apex Components’ customer portfolio. The slide should communicate that inconsistent discounting—particularly on mid-tier accounts—is eroding margin despite business growth. The central finding is a 6-percentage-point discount gap: Oak Street Industrial receives a 24% discount, compared with 18% for the company’s largest strategic account.

Use the following customer data:

Northstar Manufacturing Group: $10M revenue, $100 list price, $82 realized price, 18% discount, 41% margin
Oak Street Industrial: $8M revenue, $100 list price, $76 realized price, 24% discount, 34% margin
Pioneer Process Solutions: $1M revenue, $100 list price, $88 realized price, 12% discount, 46% margin

Explain the pattern: Oak Street receives the deepest discount despite generating less revenue than Northstar. Meanwhile, the much smaller Pioneer account is priced more tightly than either larger account. The lack of a consistent relationship between account value and discount level suggests ad hoc negotiation rather than strategic pricing.

Include these stakeholder observations as supporting evidence:

Sales Manager: “Sales reps often discount to close deals quickly, even when customers have limited alternatives.”
Finance Director: “Approval thresholds exist, but exceptions are common and not always documented.”

Conclude with the executive implication: volume is growing, but revenue remains flat because uncontrolled discount exceptions are giving away the gains. The business needs stronger approval controls and more consistent discount governance across comparable accounts.

spec.title: Discount Leakage | Inconsistent discounting erodes margin across the customer portfolio
spec.subtitle: Apex Components — Customer Discount & Margin Analysis
spec.notes: So-what: Volume is growing but revenue is flat because discount exceptions are granted without visibility or controls. Smaller customers sometimes get better pricing than strategic accounts.

Create an executive-ready business slide analyzing Q2 FY26 revenue performance by region for Datastream Analytics, comparing Q2 FY26 with Q2 FY25.

* Southeast: $9.7M → $9.4M, −3%
* Midwest: $8.0M → $7.1M, −11%

Explain the business drivers behind the regional results:

* Northeast: Growth was driven by three enterprise deals that closed in April rather than a one-time upsell. The pipeline was built over roughly nine months, suggesting the increase reflects deliberate enterprise execution rather than a windfall. Northeast revenue is $14.2M and represents approximately 33% of total revenue.
* Midwest: Performance weakened after the loss of two anchor accounts: Prism Industries ($1.4M) and Horizon Manufacturing ($0.9M), both of which cited competitor bundling. Pipeline is also materially weaker, with $2.1M of weighted pipeline versus $4.8M at the same point last year. Characterize this decline as structural rather than seasonal.
* West: Revenue increased 8% to $11.8M. Characterize this as steady, healthy growth without overstating its importance.
* Southeast: Revenue declined 3% to $9.4M. Characterize this as broadly flat and not yet a major concern.

The slide should make it immediately clear that aggregate performance looks healthier than the underlying regional picture. Emphasize the contrast between repeatable enterprise execution in the Northeast and more concerning structural weakness in the Midwest.

Keep the language concise, human, and decision-oriented. Avoid generic phrases such as ‘strong momentum,’ ‘headwinds,’ ‘mixed performance,’ or ‘strategic opportunity’ unless they add specific meaning.

cases.title: Every Machine Plays a Critical Role
cases.prompt:
Create a slide explaining why replacement parts can sustain strong pricing and margins even when the individual component appears simple or inexpensive.

Open with the idea that every part on a machine plays a critical role in keeping the broader system operational.

Consumer examples: OEM ice maker ~$98.99 vs generic ~$42.83; OEM steering pump ~$573.17 vs generic ~$198.99. OEM replacement volume ~3× generic aftermarket.

Industrial examples: Oven gas regulator ~$347, ~80% margin (downtime urgency); Aerospace bolts $150–$250/bolt, 80–90% margin (certification); Trenchless water-line $1,000–$5,000, 75–85% margin (repair consequence).

Business logic: customers pay to restore operation, avoid downtime, maintain certification, or prevent larger repair consequence — not just for the physical part.

Conclusion: replacement-part economics are driven by system criticality, supporting premium pricing and attractive margins even for simple components.

cases.title: B2B Distributor — margin leakage diagnostic
cases.prompt:
Create a consultant-style slide for evaluating where a client is losing margin and what management should do about it.

Use a hypothetical B2B distributor with approximately $500M in annual revenue.

The analysis should show that average realized price increased 2.1% over the last year, but gross margin improved only 40 bps because higher input costs and discount leakage absorbed most of the benefit. Roughly $8.4M of annual margin opportunity remains addressable.

The opportunity is concentrated in three areas: inconsistent discounting ($3.6M from tightening discount guardrails), low-value accounts priced below target ($2.7M from resetting prices), and slow cost pass-through ($2.1M from accelerating cost pass-through — 60–90 day lag).

Distinguish between structural issues (need new pricing rules) and execution issues (need better adherence to existing rules).

Recommend a practical sequence: (1) establish price corridors and approval thresholds, (2) reprice low-value accounts, (3) introduce faster cost-triggered price updates, (4) track realized price, exception rates, and margin capture weekly.

Storyline: pricing performance is improving, but inconsistent execution is leaving approximately $8M of margin on the table; most of the opportunity can be captured through tighter discount discipline and targeted repricing rather than broad-based price increases.

v5-current.title: Execution Gaps Leave $8.4M on the Table Despite 2.1% Price Gains

changes.note: New case: B2B distributor margin leakage diagnostic with $8.4M addressable opportunity across three levers

Three personas: analyst (40bps hero + lever bars + classification table), executive (full-width waterfall bridge chart as hero visual), consultant (lever bars with execution/structural badges + bridge-format findings)

Executive redesigned: replaced findings-list + hero-stat + segmented-bar with a single waterfall bridge showing $10.5M price capture → three leakage bars → $2.1M net margin — the visual IS the argument
Structural vs. execution classification badges on lever bars distinguish governance fixes from repricing decisions

cases.title: Steel Mfg — pricing value chain (expects waterfall)
cases.prompt: Show how a pricing opportunity moves from insight to realized financial impact. Explain the major stages from identifying price leakage, prioritizing opportunities, executing pricing actions, and ultimately capturing EBITDA. Include the key business outcome at each stage and call out where value is most commonly lost or delayed. Conclude with the one action leadership should take to improve conversion from identified opportunity to realized value. (Executive persona, benchmarked to a mid-market steel manufacturer, ~$500M revenue)
